# Trellis For TypeScript Consumers

Use with [the consumer guide](llms-full.txt) from the same Trellis revision.
Trellis requirements concern its own APIs and lifecycle. Configuration parsing,
validation of non-Trellis inputs, databases, DI, code layout, and local testing
tools are application choices. Neither Zod nor an ORM is required.

The npm packages `@oatscenter/trellis` and `@oatscenter/result` contain ESM
JavaScript and TypeScript declarations. Use `import`. CommonJS output and
`require()` support have intentionally been removed, with no compatibility
fallback. The shared ESM `/service` entrypoint supports Node-compatible native
runtimes, including Deno; JSR publication remains supported.

## Generate And Connect

On this unreleased Revision 7 branch, the authoritative Auth core now issues
immutable signed logical-session authority and signed retirement cutoffs.
TypeScript OAuth admission and shared connection-owned verification/revocation
caches are migrated in later phases. Do not build per-context or per-role
watchers, infer trust from missing mirror entries, or implement the retired
GrantBinding/browser-bind protocol as a fallback. Released matching libraries
remain the supported application integration until cutover completes.

Declare whole capabilities in native IDL, not individual RPC/event grants:
`required capability read;` is required and `capability export;` is optional.
Generated callers expose the selected actions. Check capability availability
before invoking an optional capability; selecting it does not mean it was approved.
Services/devices are deployable participants; apps/agents are application request
descriptors exported through the generated `apps` namespace.

Administrative Auth callers use generated actions and request their narrow
ordinary capabilities. Runtime authorization additionally requires the
applicable finite platform privilege; capability selection never confers it.
Own-authority/session maintenance uses fixed session rights. Capability discovery
does not grant authority, and capability groups are not presets expanded into
saved exact-action grants. API authors set positive `consent_revision` values;
Auth owns acceptance and action/membership introduction counters.

Retained events require trusted original JetStream publication metadata as well
as a signed publisher timestamp. Both times must lie within the authority lease,
and both must precede an ordinary revocation cutoff. Read time
is not publication evidence. Current consumer read authority is separate from
historical publisher authenticity; service code does not supply its own verifier.

Author native IDL, run `trellis update` after dependency changes, and run
`trellis generate` after IDL changes. Set `[package]`, `[sources]`, and
`[generate.typescript].output` in `trellis.toml`. For a durable `consumer`,
declare a direct `trellis` source package dependency containing
`trellis.events@v1`; select and lock its version before generation.

Import `apis` and `participants` from that one ordinary local package, for
example `import { participants } from "orders-trellis"` and the generated
participant export. There are no per-API or participant packages. Output is
executable ESM JavaScript plus declarations and `package.json`, at the source
package version, depending on the published runtime matching the CLI. No
consumer transpiler, generated Deno configuration, or runtime-path setting is
required. Configure ordinary npm dependencies or Deno import mappings yourself;
generation never edits them. Commit authored files and the lock, and commit
output when ordinary clones should build without the Trellis CLI or
source-package cache. Generation is offline once locked dependencies are
available in the validated global cache. There is no TypeScript
contract-authoring execution step.

Services import `TrellisService` from `@oatscenter/trellis/service`. Connect
with the generated participant, provisioned identity seed, and Trellis URL;
`name` is optional. Set `telemetry: false` to disable automatic telemetry.
Optional `runtime` controls service logging (including `false` to disable it),
default request timeout, event stream selection, no-responder retry, and health
heartbeat interval. Deployment/instance assignment, installed
package/participant evidence, exact grants, resources, signed context, route
JWT, and transport endpoints are resolved server-side. Authorization state is
process-memory-only and is refreshed proactively as SDK-owned maintenance.
Renewing unchanged transport authority promotes context and routing credentials
without replacing a healthy socket. Newly approved authority is adopted
automatically on a readied successor; safe accepted work keeps its receiving
connection until it settles. No manual transport-refresh API or upgrade
notification exists. Retain the logical client and still-bound resource handles
across handoffs. While own revocation coverage is unavailable, fresh application
IO either waits within its acquisition budget or reports unavailability.
Verified recovery wakes waiting acquisitions. Watch migration preserves cached
authority and existing leases; actual revocation, reduced authority, and hard
deadlines remain fail-closed. No authorization-context store or client-supplied
deployment/digest fields exist. The complete example is in
`/guides/write-a-service/service-entrypoint`.

For a participant declaring RPC `Orders.Create`, with matching generated input
and output models:

```ts
import { Result } from "@oatscenter/trellis";

await service.handleOrdersCreate(({ input }) =>
  Result.ok({ orderId: crypto.randomUUID(), customerId: input.customerId })
);
```

The UUID is just this example's application identifier. Trellis does not choose
the service's identifier scheme. Register providers, then await
`service.wait()`; stop the service with `service.stop()` during shutdown.

A caller that selects this action calls:

```ts
const order = await client.ordersCreate({ customerId: "customer-1" }).orThrow();
```

Generated flat names depend on action names and alias collisions. Inspect the
generated participant when choosing names. The old `client.rpc.orders.create`
and `service.handle.rpc.orders.create` trees are not the generated participant
interface. Dependency selections belong in IDL `use` blocks, not SDK `use(spec)`
calls.

## Handler Types And Application Dependencies

Inline handlers infer their types at registration. Extracted handlers can use
`RpcHandler<typeof participant, "Orders.Create">` from
`@oatscenter/trellis/service`. `OperationHandler`, `LiveHandler`, and
`JobHandler` and `ServiceEventHandler` provide corresponding typed boundaries.
Regenerate after an IDL change.

Handlers receive Trellis-owned arguments such as `input`, `context`, and the
scoped outbound `client`. Trellis does not inject application dependencies. A
closure is one way to supply a database or domain function; an application can
use its own DI system to construct that closure.

Every public service handler receives the same flat, contract-selected
`ServiceHandlerClient<typeof participant>` as its `client`. It exposes selected
outbound RPC, Operation, Live, and Event-publish methods, owned Event publishers
with `.prepare(...)`, bound `kv`, `store`, and `jobs` handles,
`connection`/`name`, and `availability()`, `watchAvailability()`,
`publishPrepared(...)`, and `transfer(...)`. Registration and lifecycle methods
stay on the connected service; there is no generic
`client.rpc`/`client.operation`/`client.event` tree.

Declare wire models and expected errors in IDL. The generator owns the runtime
schemas and generated error types. Handlers can return declared errors through
`Result.err(...)`; callers can distinguish them from runtime/transport failures.
`.orThrow()` converts a failed result to an exception where that matches the
application's control flow. Native cursor-paginated RPCs add lazy `.pages()` and
`.items()` iterators. Missing `nextCursor` is the sole end signal; general
keyset pagination does not promise a snapshot.

## Events And Live observations

For a declared event `Orders.Changed`, generated service methods include
`publishOrdersChanged(...)` and, when selected, `onOrdersChanged(...)`:

```ts
await service.onOrdersChanged(({ event }) => {
  console.log(event);
  return Result.ok(undefined);
}).orThrow();
```

The `event` is the typed payload; `context` carries runtime metadata. Durable
delivery comes from declared Consumer resources. The runtime owns durable
identity, local concurrency, retry, proof verification, and scoped Events DLQ.
Subjects include the encoded qualified API identity and base64url parameter
tokens; the message proof binds the exact API, dotted event name, and parameter
count. Handler success is acknowledged only after it completes; final exhaustion
is durably recorded before source acknowledgement. Manual replay uses the same
handler with a fresh retry budget, does not rewind the original Consumer, and
durably resolves before acknowledgement. A normal publish happens immediately;
it is not a database commit fence.

Live providers receive an abort signal. Stop connection-scoped work when it
aborts, and close or abort a caller subscription when no longer needed. A caller
subscription is an owned async iterator: call `return()`/`throw()` or abort its
signal to release it, and disposal is idempotent even before the first `next()`.
Live observations and Operation watchers are authorized live sessions negotiated
with bounded opening requests; provider frames are signed and control responses
bind the session ID, logical command sequence, and command hash. A session has
protocol liveness and credit bounds, not a total age or message cap. Closing
returns a receipt whose remote-cleanup state is complete, incomplete, or
unconfirmed.

## Operations And Jobs

For operation `Reports.Generate`:

```ts
const operation = await client.reportsGenerate(input).start().orThrow();
const terminal = await operation.wait().orThrow();
if (terminal.state === "completed") console.log(terminal.output);
```

The provider registers through its generated participant facade. A watcher is a
separate live observation session: open it before reading the current snapshot,
expect ordered transient updates and a terminal state after reconciliation, and
treat a transport interruption as an observation error rather than an invented
terminal state. Closing a watcher leaves the durable work running. Acceptance,
progress, signals, cancellation, and terminal state use the durable repository.
Get, watch, signal, and cancel remain bound to the creator principal and
participant across reconnects. Completed, failed, and cancelled states cannot be
changed. Transfer-capable invocations return a transfer-aware result; consult
its generated type rather than assuming the ordinary operation result shape.
`TransportError` code `trellis.request.unavailable` with `noResponders: true`
means the target service is not responding, not that an offer is malformed or
the durable operation failed. Restore service reachability and retry observation
of the same operation; do not start replacement business work. RPC uses the same
unavailable classification. The generated
`service.handleReportsGenerate.control(id)` returns a typed owner-fenced local
handle; non-owners cannot borrow the fence. Use
`service.handleReportsGenerate.reconcile(id)` from another service replica to
ask the current owner to re-enter the handler with stored input, caller, and
durable progress. The handler's `signal` aborts on cancellation or ownership
loss; await cleanup of side-effecting children before returning. Caller
`operation.cancel()` returns terminal `Cancelled` only after this cleanup and
the fenced terminal write. Stalled cleanup remains nonterminal and
lease-renewed. Throwing, returning an error, or `op.defer()` does not
acknowledge successful cleanup. Reconciliation or recovery re-enters the
registered handler with its signal already aborted; check that signal and
perform cleanup before business work. Return successfully only after cleanup is
complete. Ownership loss also aborts the signal, but a stale executor cannot
finalize cancellation.

For upload Operations, use the generated `.transfer(body).start()` workflow.
The provider consumes runtime-staged bytes with `transfer.stream()` or
`transfer.bytes()`, and starts processing only after backend and durable Operation
transfer commit. Receive grants use the high-level transfer helper's `stream()`
for large bodies or `bytes()` for a collected buffer. Transfer v2 moves raw bytes
over bounded one-way NATS windows; Web Streams backpressure/backend consumption
drives cumulative credit, not a per-chunk RPC. Credit does not report upload
success. Durable watch transfer progress is monotonic and may be coalesced, with
exact final `transferredBytes`; `chunkIndex`/`chunkBytes` describe the latest
credited frame represented rather than one event per frame. Grants hide physical
storage protocols and credentials. Authority growth retains an in-flight
transfer's admitting generation; physical disconnect interrupts it, and an
uncommitted upload restarts from byte zero.
The connection `timeout` covers transfer activation from transport acquisition
through the provider reply, and separately bounds cancellation; it is not a body
lifetime limit. A cancellation timeout releases local ownership but does not
confirm remote cleanup. Once durable commit is underway, wire cancellation
cannot promise an uncommitted outcome. A lost commit reply retains staged bytes;
resume the Operation to reconcile its durable result before retrying.

For an ordinary TypeScript operation, cancellation-first admission uses
`.start(undefined, { invocationId, cancellationRequested: true })` with a
caller-chosen ULID and the same frozen input on every retry. Both Invoke and
Cancel authority are required before durable reservation. The cancellation
intent is atomic with fresh admission, merges into an exact existing invocation,
and cannot be cleared by a normal start replay. Terminal replays remain
unchanged. Native cancellation-first admission also supports upload operations,
without opening upload staging. Handler `transfer` is therefore optional: handle
already-aborted cleanup before accessing it, and require a transfer handle on
the ordinary upload branch. The TypeScript transfer-start builder does not
expose the cancellation-first option because its result describes an actual
transfer.

Private queues are available as `service.jobs.<queue>`. Register handlers with
`handle(...)`, create work with `create(...)`, and observe the returned job
reference. Retry and automatic delivery acknowledgement are runtime-owned.
Worker concurrency is local; optional keyed concurrency is a declared semantic
policy. Waiting for keyed capacity maintains the current delivery and does not
consume an attempt before the handler starts. `Jobs.Summary` computes matching
totals, groups, and statistics independently of a `Jobs.Query` page. Live
updates are separate from durable progress and terminal results. Job deadlines
are creation-relative. Omitted retry means five ordinary attempts with delays of
5s, 30s, 2m, and 10m; explicit retry requires exactly one fewer positive ordered
backoffs than total attempts. Broker redelivery is unlimited. Before business
work, check `job.signal.aborted`: already-aborted job handlers must reconcile
earlier side effects. Cleanup errors preserve redelivery; previously started
work reaches Expired or Dead only after successful cleanup. Never-started
expiration confirms terminal publication before releasing its recovered key
slot, without running the handler. Publication failure retains the reservation;
terminal redelivery reconciles remaining slots before acknowledgement. Ordinary
queues use Block, not an authored stale policy. Coordinator fail-stale takeover
preserves cleanup for a recovered owner with a fresh fence and
`job.signal.reason === "stale-attempt"`; only that owner settles Stale, without
mutating the replacement owner's slot. Ignored stale completions are nonterminal
diagnostics and retain redelivery until cleanup settles. A never-started
displaced reservation settles Pending to Stale without handler execution.

Lifecycle publication awaits JetStream acknowledgement. Typed live updates
remain transient and do not require a durable stream.

Execution state and attempts follow accepted lifecycle transitions in broker
stream-sequence order. Created initializes but cannot reopen a job. Diagnostics,
heartbeats, logs, and progress cannot override settlement or attempts. A valid
Retried opens a new run under the same ID without deleting history. Work retains
its original lifecycle sequence through broker source metadata. Old-run
deliveries are acknowledged without touching newer-run coordination. Deferred
work rereads lifecycle state before acquisition.

## Resources And Transactional Events

Use generated State, KV, Store, Consumer, and Job handles. State is one typed
value without key/TTL; KV is typed history; Store is raw bytes. State/KV
historical migration runs in SDK memory without write-on-read. These are
Trellis-managed handles, not an application database abstraction.

Use Store entry `stream()` for large bodies. Shared Store reads pull finite,
byte-capped batches on demand and verify chunk order/count, size, and SHA-256
before successful EOF; partial output is not a verified complete object.
`bytes()` consumes the same reader but retains the entire object in memory.
Paused reads recreate expired backend consumers at the exact next chunk while
the pinned connection and stored chunks remain available. Streams fail on
physical disconnect or closure, and consumer cleanup precedes generation-lease
release. Native ObjectStore links are unsupported.

`TypedStore.list(...)` and file metadata lists use key-sorted keyset pagination
with opaque cursors bound to the prefix query. The limit defaults to 100 and
must be at most 500; only absent `nextCursor` means completion. Desired resource
capacities are sizing hints, approved commitments are authority, and runtime
handles expose observed provider limits. Trellis does not adopt or destroy
foreign-owned physical resources.

When SQL writes and event/job intents need one atomic commit, configure
`service.createSqlOutbox(...)` with `dialect`, an `executor`, and a
`transaction` runner. The transaction runner supplies the application's `tx` and
a transaction-scoped `SqlExecutor`:

```ts
await outbox.transaction(async ({ tx, event, job }) => {
  await orders.markShipped(tx, orderId);
  await event.orders.shipped.enqueue({ orderId }).orThrow();
}).orThrow();
```

Here `orders` and `tx` belong to the application. The transaction-scoped event
tree is an outbox API, unlike ordinary flat publish methods. Normal event
facades do not expose `enqueue`. Job submission intents use the callback's `job`
tree. `getSqlOutboxMigrations(...)` returns Trellis helper-table migration
artifacts for the application's migration tool to apply.

Applications adapt their chosen database and transaction handles to the generic
`SqlExecutor` interface; Trellis does not provide ORM-specific adapters. NATS KV
outbox/inbox helpers do not provide atomicity with unrelated SQL writes.

SQL and NATS KV outbox claims expire after 30 seconds. `claimDue(...)` returns
the claimed records; pass a record, not just its ID, to `markDispatched(...)` or
`markFailed(...)`. These return false when a newer claim superseded that record.
KV acquisition/completion uses revision CAS. Dispatch may publish again after
interruption, so consumers must handle duplicates. SQL inbox `record()` returns
true only for the call that inserted the ID. Commit that marker with a domain
side effect when both need to be atomic.

The schema helpers create current tables; they do not upgrade pre-release
layouts. Apply any required migration with the application's migration tooling
before using a retained older database.

## Browser Apps And Verification

For live Deno tests, `await using runtime = await TrellisTestRuntime.start()`
from `@oatscenter/trellis-testkit` acquires exact-version production CLI/server
archives pinned by SHA-256, currently for Linux x86-64 only. No installed Trellis executables or nsc are
required. Production commands generate config and own managed NATS in a private
sandbox with seeded admin. Network is needed on first use;
`TRELLIS_TEST_CACHE_DIR` reuses verified binaries only. Use
`trellis: { source: { kind: "path", cli, server } }` for an exact-version
prebuilt pair, with no fallback. `restart()` retains data/identity and restarts
the full host and broker. Stop first requests graceful host shutdown; on timeout
or host exit, isolated process-group cleanup reclaims remaining owned children
before sandbox removal. Startup requires `/readyz` metadata's `processId` to
match the spawned native host, not another runtime at the selected port.
`firstAdmin: "browser-flow"` opts into browser setup.
The Rust testkit links the same production runtime in-process instead.

Browser apps use
`TrellisClient.connect({ participant, trellisUrl, auth:
"browser" })` or the
[Svelte integration](llms-svelte.txt). Let the Trellis client own its auth
installation, proactive refresh, transport maintenance, and normal `logout()`.
Use the connected client's `logout()` for sign-out, not the generated
`sessionsLogout()` alone: session revocation can close the connection before its
RPC reply arrives. The helper confirms `session_revoked` through signed HTTP
recovery if needed; other authorization failures remain failures.

Browser sign-in transports a reusable signed intent (`intentId`, opaque
`intent`, and `loginUrl`), not an already-running authentication attempt. The
portal verifies the intent on render; authentication starts a bounded,
independently bound transaction. Callbacks carry `transactionId`.
`ClientAuthContinuation` supports `{ status: "bound", transactionId }` for
caller-owned completion or `{ status: "handled" }` for caller-owned routing. Do
not fabricate login metadata or authorization from a callback.

Custom portals use the public browser-auth helpers `portalIntentFromUrl`,
`portalTransactionIdFromUrl`, `fetchPortalIntentState`, and
`startPortalTransaction`. Retain the intent across attempt expiry and start a
new transaction when the user continues; do not send the user back to the app
just to restart. The portal receives no initiating app private key. Its fresh
transaction binding is separate from the app's key-bound completion proof.
Portal progress requires that raw binding. Persist a pending binding indexed by
intent before `startPortalTransaction`; reuse it on retry or reload, then
associate it with the returned transaction ID. A same-binding retry recovers the
active transaction without resetting state or expiry; another binding receives
`intent_transaction_active` and must not displace it.
Public intent rendering never returns transaction discovery. Detached discovery
uses the initiating key's fresh `userAuthProgress` session proof at
`/auth/intents/progress` and receives a transaction ID only when ready to bind.
Browser OIDC uses `portalProviderLoginUrl()` to POST JSON transaction inputs and
navigate to the returned provider URL; first and replayed callbacks return to
the portal with `transactionId`. Reuse compatible approved grants without
prompting again; expanded authority eligible for approval requests current
consent after authentication. Preserve stable authorization errors with a valid
login rather than automatically starting another login. The SDK owns those
recovery decisions.

A generated device companion is established only through the parent device's
activation flow and separate user consent. It has its own ordinary App/Agent
session and cannot use standalone bootstrap or the parent device's authority.

For real-runtime tests, use the Deno `TrellisTestRuntime` package and generated
participants. See `/guides/testing-trellis-services` for a complete test rather
than constructing handwritten bootstrap responses. The application's other tests
remain its own choice. Regenerate SDKs, then run that repository's checks.
